To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the effective gravitational coupling G is a dynamical field that can be calculated from a renormalizable quantum field theory in curved spacetime and that it is a function of the Newtonian potential, which is a function of space and time, and that the effective action approach leads to a small G variation that can explain galaxy rotation curves and dispersion profiles without the need for dark matter.

RGGR can be applied to the galaxy context, that it can explain the galaxy rotation curves and dispersion profiles without the need for dark matter, and that the results are of comparable quality to the best phenomenological models, and significantly better that the NFW profile and MOND.

the study of the RG effects to gravity, in particular in the galaxy context.

the study of the gravitational field of galaxies, and the comparison of the results obtained with the predictions of General Relativity, MOND and the Newtonian dark matter profiles NFW and Burkert.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, while MOND is not ruled out, it is certainly not the only possible solution to the dark matter problem.
the phenomenological dark matter models are still the best available models, but RGGR is the most promising theoretical candidate to explain dark matter phenomenology.
, in the context of the effective action approach, RG gravity is a promising alternative to dark matter in galaxies, and in particular for elliptical galaxies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
RGGR can be used as a phenomenological dark matter alternative.
, even with the simplest RG improvement of gravity, the phenomenology of galaxies is significantly improved.
RGGR is able to explain most of the phenomenology of galaxies, including the rotation curves, the dispersion curves and the velocity anisotropy, without the need of dark matter.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the RG effects in General Relativity, even if they do not explain all the phenomenology, are a promising avenue of research to understand the origin of dark matter and the dark sector in general.

the RG effects in the effective action approach, in the weak-field regime, are very small and can be treated perturbatively, but are still large enough to generate the observed galaxy rotation curves and dispersion curves.
the RG effects in gravity, which are not included in the standard General Relativity, can provide an explanation for the dark matter phenomenology in disk and elliptical systems.
